summary.text: Antarctic bottom water is the densest water mass in the oceans, a Southern Ocean water at −0.8 to 2 °C that fills ocean basins below 4000 m.
It forms at the surface along Antarctica's coast, where winter sea ice growth leaves salty brine behind and cold air chills the water until it is dense enough to sink.
Sliding down the continental slope and north along the seafloor, it forms the lower branch of the thermohaline circulation, and melting ice has slowed its formation.

facts.label: Where it sits
facts.value: Below 4000 m in basins linked to the Southern Ocean

facts.label: Ice from coastal polynyas
facts.value: About 2,000 km³ of sea ice in one season

items.prompt: Seawater along the Antarctic coast freezes into new sea ice on a winter night. What happens to the liquid water left just beneath the ice?

options.label: It turns fresher and floats up to the surface
It turns saltier and heavier, so it sinks
It warms up and spreads out along the coast
It stays exactly as salty and heavy as before

items.explain: Freezing leaves salt behind in the water below, and with the cold air this makes the surface water denser so it can sink.

items.prompt: Across most of the southern hemisphere, Antarctic bottom water lies underneath every other deep water mass. Why does it end up at the very bottom?

options.label: It holds more oxygen than other water
It moves faster than the water above it
It is the heaviest water in the open ocean
It is pulled down by the shape of the seabed

items.explain: It is the densest water in the open ocean, so it slides beneath the other bottom and intermediate waters.

items.prompt: Unlike most deep water, this water mass starts out at the sea surface before it sinks. What does starting at the surface allow it to do?

options.label: Swap large amounts of heat and gases with the air
Stay warmer than all other deep ocean water
Avoid mixing with any other water on its way
Lose its salt before it reaches the seafloor

items.explain: Because it forms near the surface, it exchanges large quantities of heat and gases with the atmosphere before sinking.

items.prompt: Cold winds blowing off Antarctica push freshly formed sea ice away from the shore. How does this help make more dense bottom water?

options.label: It lets warm currents reach the shore and heat the water
It piles the ice up so that it melts into fresh water
It shields the sea from the cold winter air
It opens water to freezing air, so more ice forms

items.explain: Clearing the ice opens patches of water, called polynyas, to the cold winter air, which forms more sea ice and makes the water saltier and colder.

items.prompt: In the Amundsen Sea, the open-water patches that make dense water have weakened so much that dense water barely forms. What has happened to the nearby ice shelves?

options.label: They have grown thicker as the sea cooled
They have stayed the same size as before
They have started to retreat and may collapse
They have frozen solid down to the seabed

items.explain: These polynyas normally keep warm deep water away from the base of ice shelves; where they have weakened, the shelves have begun to retreat.

items.prompt: Melting ice sheets pour extra fresh water into the seas around Antarctica. What does this do to the making of bottom water?

options.label: It speeds it up by adding more water
It has no effect on how much forms
It moves all of it to the Arctic
It slows it, since the water is less salty

items.explain: Surface water must be very cold and salty to become deep water, and melting ice has slowed the formation of this water mass.
